components.note: 钅 (metal) — potassium is a metallic element, so 钾 uses the metal radical.
甲 (jiǎ) gives the sound — an exact match with 钾's reading.

example.hanzi: 香蕉含有丰富的钾。
example.pinyin: Xiāngjiāo hányǒu fēngfù de jiǎ.
example.english: Bananas contain abundant potassium.
example.fact: Potassium is essential for nerve signaling and muscle contraction in the human body, and bananas are one of the best-known dietary sources of it.

components.note: 日 (sun) — 暧 originally described dim, hazy light, extended figuratively to obscurity and ambiguity.
爱 (ài) gives the sound — an exact match with 暧's reading.

example.hanzi: 他们两个人的关系很暧昧。
example.pinyin: Tāmen liǎng gè rén de guānxi hěn àimèi.
example.english: The relationship between the two of them is very ambiguous.
example.fact: 暧 almost never appears alone — it exists mainly in the word 暧昧 (àimèi), describing a relationship or situation that is deliberately unclear, often romantically.

components.note: 贝 (shell/money) is the traditional semantic root, though the link to 赓's modern meaning 'to continue' is not transparent today — one of many characters whose original semantic logic has been lost over time.
庚 (gēng) gives the sound — an exact match with 赓's reading.

example.hanzi: 我们要赓续这一光荣传统。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen yào gēngxù zhè yī guāngróng chuántǒng.
example.english: We must continue this glorious tradition.
example.fact: 赓 is a literary character used almost exclusively in the formal compound 赓续 (gēngxù, "to continue, carry on"), favored in political and ceremonial speech rather than everyday conversation.

etymologyHint: A hand 又 holding up a candle, representing failing vision

components.note: 又 depicts a hand; the ancient form of 叟 showed a hand holding up a torch or candle, an image later applied to elderly men whose failing eyes needed extra light.

example.hanzi: 那位老叟坐在门口晒太阳。
example.pinyin: Nà wèi lǎosǒu zuò zài ménkǒu shài tàiyáng.
example.english: That old man sat at the doorway sunbathing.
example.fact: 叟 is a literary word for "old man," most familiar today in the idiom 童叟无欺 (tóng sǒu wú qī, "cheating neither children nor the elderly"), traditionally displayed by honest shopkeepers.

etymologyHint: To lose 失 a person 亻

components.note: 亻 (person) — 佚 originally depicted a person going missing.
失 (to lose) — combined with 'person,' gives the sense of someone who has fled or gone missing, extended to 'idle, dissolute' and used as a surname.

example.hanzi: 这首诗的作者佚名。
example.pinyin: Zhè shǒu shī de zuòzhě yìmíng.
example.english: The author of this poem is anonymous/unknown.
example.fact: 佚名 (yìmíng, literally "name lost") is the standard label Chinese museums, books, and art collections use for works whose creator is unknown — comparable to "anonymous" in English.

meanings: classifier for sheets of papers etc: pile, pad

example.hanzi: 桌子上放着一沓纸。
example.pinyin: Zhuōzi shàng fàngzhe yí dá zhǐ.
example.english: There is a stack of paper on the table.
example.fact: As a measure word, 沓 (dá) counts thick stacks of flat things like paper or documents — 一沓 (yí dá) is the standard way to say "a stack of paper" in Chinese office language.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 撂 describes an action done with the hands, like putting something down.
畧 (lüè, a variant of 略) gives a sound now quite distant from 撂's reading liào — a colloquial northern-dialect character whose phonetic link has drifted far over time.

example.hanzi: 他把书包往地上一撂就走了。
example.pinyin: Tā bǎ shūbāo wǎng dì shàng yī liào jiù zǒule.
example.english: He tossed his backpack onto the ground and left.
example.fact: 撂 is a colloquial northern-Mandarin verb for dropping something down carelessly, and appears in the common phrase 撂狠话 (liào hěnhuà, "to throw out harsh words or threats").

components.note: 虫 (insect) — 蛊 describes venomous creatures and the poison or black magic associated with them.

皿 (mǐn) is listed as this character's phonetic element, though its reading is quite far from 蛊's gǔ — the traditional image of insects massed inside a vessel (皿) may be closer to the character's real origin than a sound cue.

example.hanzi: 古代传说中,蛊是一种毒虫。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài chuánshuō zhōng, gǔ shì yī zhǒng dú chóng.
example.english: In ancient legend, 蛊 was a kind of venomous insect.
example.fact: 蛊 refers to a legendary poison said to be brewed from venomous insects sealed in a jar, giving rise to 蛊惑 (gǔhuò, "to bewitch, to mislead"), still used today for someone who deceives others.

components.note: 男 (male/boy) — 甥 refers to a sister's son, a male relative.
生 (shēng) gives the sound — an exact match with 甥's reading.

example.hanzi: 他是我姐姐的儿子,我的外甥。
example.pinyin: Tā shì wǒ jiějiě de érzi, wǒ de wàishēng.
example.english: He is my older sister's son, my nephew.
example.fact: Chinese kinship terms distinguish a sister's son (外甥, wàishēng) from a brother's son (侄子, zhízi) — two completely different words, unlike English "nephew," which covers both.

components.note: 王 (the 玉 jade radical in its component form) — 璐 names a type of fine jade.
路 (lù) gives the sound — an exact match with 璐's reading.

example.hanzi: 她的名字叫"李璐"。
example.pinyin: Tā de míngzi jiào "Lǐ Lù".
example.english: Her name is "Li Lu."
example.fact: 璐 means "fine jade" but appears almost exclusively as a character chosen for personal names, since parents favor jade-related characters for their precious, auspicious connotations.

etymologyHint: A woman safe in a house 安 at sunset 日

components.note: 日 (sun) — used together with 安 to describe a peaceful sunset, and by extension, lateness in the day.
安 (peaceful, safe) — combined with 'sun,' gives 晏 the sense of calm, and later 'late,' as in 晏起 (yànqǐ, "to rise late").

example.hanzi: 晏子是春秋时期著名的政治家。
example.pinyin: Yànzǐ shì Chūnqiū shíqī zhùmíng de zhèngzhìjiā.
example.english: Yanzi was a famous statesman of the Spring and Autumn period.
example.fact: 晏 is best known today as the surname of 晏子 (Yanzi), a renowned statesman and diplomat of the Spring and Autumn period (770–476 BC), celebrated for his wit in the classic text 晏子春秋.

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — 瘪 describes something shriveled or wasted, as if depleted by illness.
自 (zì) is marked as the phonetic element, though its reading is quite distant from 瘪's biě — the sound connection has drifted far from the modern pronunciation.

example.hanzi: 这个球瘪了,不能用了。
example.pinyin: Zhège qiú biěle, bù néng yòngle.
example.english: This ball is deflated and can't be used.
example.fact: 瘪 is the standard character for something deflated or shrunken, from tires and balls to a gaunt face, as in 干瘪 (gānbiě, "withered, shriveled").

meanings: name of a river in Henan

components.note: 氵 (water) — 漳 names a river.
章 (zhāng) gives the sound — an exact match with 漳's reading.

example.hanzi: 漳州是福建省的一个城市。
example.pinyin: Zhāngzhōu shì Fújiàn Shěng de yí gè chéngshì.
example.english: Zhangzhou is a city in Fujian province.
example.fact: 漳 names the Zhang River (漳江) in Fujian, and gives its name to the city of 漳州 (Zhangzhou), a major port city facing Taiwan across the strait.

components.note: 门 (gate) — eunuchs traditionally served and guarded the gates and inner chambers of the imperial palace.
奄 (yǎn) gives a sound close to 阉's reading yān, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 古代皇宫里有很多阉人。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài huánggōng lǐ yǒu hěn duō yānrén.
example.english: In ancient times, there were many eunuchs in the imperial palace.
example.fact: 阉 refers to castration, historically most associated with 太监 (tàijiàn, "eunuchs") who served in the Chinese imperial palace, a practice documented for over two thousand years.

components.note: 足 (foot) — 蹂 describes trampling with the feet.
柔 (róu) gives the sound — an exact match with 蹂's reading.

example.hanzi: 侵略者蹂躏了当地的百姓。
example.pinyin: Qīnlüèzhě róulìnle dāngdì de bǎixìng.
example.english: The invaders trampled on the local people.
example.fact: 蹂躏 (róulìn) originally described livestock trampling grass underfoot, but today is used mostly in the metaphorical sense of trampling on people's rights or dignity.

components.note: 鱼 (fish) — 鳃 names the breathing organ of fish.
思 (sī) gives a sound related to 鳃's reading sāi, sharing the initial consonant but with the vowel shifted over time.

example.hanzi: 鱼用鳃呼吸。
example.pinyin: Yú yòng sāi hūxī.
example.english: Fish breathe using their gills.
example.fact: Fish gills (鳃) extract dissolved oxygen directly from water, letting fish breathe without ever surfacing — a fundamentally different respiratory system from lungs.

meanings: vessel used to hold grain offerings
sacrificial vessel used for grain offerings

components.note: 王 (jade) — 琏 names a jade-adorned ceremonial vessel used for grain offerings.
连 (lián) gives a sound close to 琏's reading liǎn, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 贾琏是《红楼梦》里的一个人物。
example.pinyin: Jiǎ Liǎn shì "Hónglóumèng" lǐ de yí gè rénwù.
example.english: Jia Lian is a character in "Dream of the Red Chamber."
example.fact: 琏 is a rare character best known today from 贾琏 (Jiǎ Liǎn), a character in the classic 18th-century novel 红楼梦 (Dream of the Red Chamber), one of China's Four Great Classical Novels.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 湃 describes the sound and surge of waves.
拜 (bài) gives a sound close to 湃's reading pài, differing only in whether the initial consonant is aspirated.

example.hanzi: 海浪澎湃,声音很大。
example.pinyin: Hǎilàng pēngpài, shēngyīn hěn dà.
example.english: The sea waves surged, and the sound was very loud.
example.fact: 湃 is a bound character appearing almost exclusively in 澎湃 (pēngpài), a word for surging waves that is also used figuratively for strong, turbulent emotion, as in 心潮澎湃 ("one's feelings surge").

meanings: used in 轆轆|辘辘[lu4 lu4]
used in 軲轆|轱辘[gu1 lu5] and 轂轆|毂辘[gu1 lu5]

components.note: 车 (cart/wheel) — 辘 names a wheeled mechanism, a windlass or pulley.
鹿 (lù) gives the sound — an exact match with 辘's reading.

example.hanzi: 他饿得饥肠辘辘。
example.pinyin: Tā è de jīcháng lùlù.
example.english: He was so hungry his stomach was rumbling.
example.fact: 辘辘 imitates the rumbling sound of wheels turning, and this sound image was extended to describe a hungry, growling stomach in the common idiom 饥肠辘辘 (jīcháng lùlù).

components.note: 亻 (person) — 僭 describes a person overstepping their proper rank or authority.
朁 (a rare character usually read cǎn) gives a sound now quite distant from 僭's reading jiàn — the phonetic link has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 他僭越了自己的职权。
example.pinyin: Tā jiànyuèle zìjǐ de zhíquán.
example.english: He overstepped his authority.
example.fact: 僭 is a classical-Chinese term for overstepping one's proper rank, seen today mainly in 僭越 (jiànyuè), a formal word for exceeding one's authority — historically a serious charge in a hierarchical imperial court.

meanings: used in 蹂躪|蹂躏[rou2 lin4]

components.note: 足 (foot) — 躏 describes trampling underfoot.
蔺 (lìn) gives the sound — an exact match with 躏's reading.

example.hanzi: 人权不应该受到蹂躏。
example.pinyin: Rénquán bù yīnggāi shòudào róulìn.
example.english: Human rights should not be trampled upon.
example.fact: 躏 never appears alone in modern Chinese — it exists solely as the second half of 蹂躏 (róulìn, "to trample, to violate"), a clear example of a character that survives only inside one fixed compound.

components.note: 鼻 (nose) — snoring is produced through the nose and mouth during sleep.
干 (gān) gives a sound related to 鼾's reading hān, sharing the final but with the initial consonant shifted.

example.hanzi: 他打鼾打得很响。
example.pinyin: Tā dǎhān dǎ de hěn xiǎng.
example.english: He snores very loudly.
example.fact: Snoring (打鼾, dǎhān) happens when relaxed throat tissue partially blocks the airway during sleep — when severe and paired with breathing pauses, it can signal sleep apnea.

components.note: 忄 (heart/mind) — 懵 describes a confused, muddled state of mind.
瞢 (méng) gives a sound close to 懵's reading měng, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他被这个问题问懵了。
example.pinyin: Tā bèi zhège wèntí wèn měngle.
example.english: He was left dumbfounded by this question.
example.fact: 懵 is common in modern internet slang as 懵了 (měngle) or the meme phrase 一脸懵 ("a face full of confusion"), a good example of an old literary character gaining new life online.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — a sickle is a metal farming tool.
廉 (lián) gives the sound — an exact match with 镰's reading.

example.hanzi: 农民用镰刀割麦子。
example.pinyin: Nóngmín yòng liándāo gē màizi.
example.english: Farmers use sickles to cut wheat.
example.fact: The sickle (镰刀, liándāo) is one of humanity's oldest agricultural tools, and its crossed image with a hammer became a globally recognized 20th-century political symbol.

etymologyHint: A bed 爿 in a house 宀; 未 provides the pronunciation

components.note: 宀 (roof/house) — sleep happens indoors, at home.
爿 (a bed, as in half of 床) — combined with 'roof,' pictures someone sleeping in bed at home. The full character also contains 未, which historically supplied the pronunciation.

example.hanzi: 他夜不能寐,一直在想着这件事。
example.pinyin: Tā yè bù néng mèi, yīzhí zài xiǎngzhe zhè jiàn shì.
example.english: He couldn't sleep at night, constantly thinking about this matter.
example.fact: 寐 is a literary word for sleep best known from the idiom 夜不能寐 (yè bù néng mèi, "unable to sleep at night") and from 梦寐以求 (mèngmèi yǐqiú, "to long for something even in one's dreams").

components.note: 衤 (clothing) — 褚's original meaning involved padded clothing or a cloth bag.
者 (zhě) gives a sound related to 褚's reading chǔ, sharing the tone but with the consonant and vowel shifted over time.

example.hanzi: 褚遂良是唐朝著名的书法家。
example.pinyin: Chǔ Suìliáng shì Tángcháo zhùmíng de shūfǎjiā.
example.english: Chu Suiliang was a famous calligrapher of the Tang dynasty.
example.fact: 褚 survives today mainly as a surname, most famously that of 褚遂良 (Chu Suiliang, 596–658), one of the most celebrated calligraphers of the Tang dynasty, still studied by calligraphy students.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 攥 describes gripping tightly with the hand.
纂 (zuǎn) gives a sound close to 攥's reading zuàn, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他紧紧地攥着那张纸条。
example.pinyin: Tā jǐnjǐn de zuànzhe nà zhāng zhǐtiáo.
example.english: He tightly clutched that slip of paper.
example.fact: 攥 is a colloquial, everyday verb for gripping something tightly in one's fist, much more common in spoken Mandarin than in formal writing.

etymologyHint: A stream 氵 flowing through a valley 间; 间 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 氵 (water) — represents flowing water; 涧 names a mountain brook.
间 (between, gap) — depicts the gap between mountains, a valley, through which the stream flows; 间 (jiàn) also happens to be an exact-sounding match for 涧's pronunciation.

example.hanzi: 山间有一条清澈的溪涧。
example.pinyin: Shānjiān yǒu yī tiáo qīngchè de xījiàn.
example.english: There is a clear mountain stream between the mountains.
example.fact: 涧 specifically names a stream running through a mountain valley or gorge, distinct from 河 (a general river) or 溪 (a small brook not necessarily set in a valley).

components.note: 虫 (insect/small creature) — in old classification schemes, bats were grouped with insects and other small creatures rather than mammals.
扁 (biǎn) gives a sound very close to 蝙's reading biān, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 蝙蝠喜欢在夜里活动。
example.pinyin: Biānfú xǐhuan zài yèlǐ huódòng.
example.english: Bats like to be active at night.
example.fact: Bats (蝙蝠, biānfú) are the only mammals capable of true, sustained flight, and many species navigate in the dark using echolocation.

meanings: (bound form) the belly flap of a crab; apron

components.note: ⺼ (flesh/body, the 肉 radical) — 脐 names a body part, the navel.
齐 (qí) gives the sound — an exact match with 脐's reading.

example.hanzi: 婴儿出生后要剪断脐带。
example.pinyin: Yīng'ér chūshēng hòu yào jiǎnduàn qídài.
example.english: After a baby is born, the umbilical cord must be cut.
example.fact: The umbilical cord (脐带, qídài) is a baby's only lifeline for oxygen and nutrients before birth, and the belly button (肚脐, dùqí) is simply the scar left after it's cut.

meanings: shaft of a cart or carriage

components.note: 车 (cart) — 辕 names a structural part of a cart or carriage.
袁 (yuán) gives the sound — an exact match with 辕's reading.

example.hanzi: 古代马车前面有两根车辕。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài mǎchē qiánmiàn yǒu liǎng gēn chēyuán.
example.english: Ancient horse carriages had two shafts in front.
example.fact: 辕 names the long shafts extending forward from a cart to which draft animals are harnessed, a part of traditional horse-drawn carriage design predating motor vehicles by millennia.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 涣 originally described water dispersing or scattering.
奂 (huàn) gives the sound — an exact match with 涣's reading.

example.hanzi: 长期没有训练,队伍变得涣散了。
example.pinyin: Chángqī méiyǒu xùnliàn, duìwu biàn de huànsànle.
example.english: Without training for a long time, the team became disorganized and lacking cohesion.
example.fact: 涣 survives in modern Chinese almost exclusively in 涣散 (huànsàn), a word for scattered morale or lax discipline, often used in the set phrase 军心涣散 ("the troops' morale has collapsed").

meanings: Qi, a Zhou Dynasty vassal state

components.note: 木 (tree) — 杞 names a woody plant, the wolfberry shrub.
己 (jǐ) gives a sound close to 杞's reading qǐ, sharing the final and tone but differing in the initial consonant.

example.hanzi: 你不要杞人忧天了。
example.pinyin: Nǐ bùyào qǐ rén yōu tiān le.
example.english: Don't worry needlessly (lit. "don't be the man of Qi who feared the sky would fall").
example.fact: 杞人忧天 (qǐ rén yōu tiān) comes from an ancient parable about a man from the small state of Qi who couldn't sleep or eat for fear the sky would collapse — still the standard Chinese idiom for baseless anxiety.

etymologyHint: A dazzling 昱 flame 火; 昱 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 火 (fire) — represents flame; 煜 describes something bright and shining, like firelight.
昱 (bright, radiant) — combined with 'fire,' intensifies the sense of dazzling brightness. 昱 (yù) is also an exact phonetic match for 煜's reading.

example.hanzi: 李煜是南唐的最后一位皇帝,也是著名词人。
example.pinyin: Lǐ Yù shì Nán Táng de zuìhòu yī wèi huángdì, yěshì zhùmíng círén.
example.english: Li Yu was the last emperor of Southern Tang, and also a famous poet.
example.fact: 煜 is a common name character for its meaning "radiant, shining," most famously borne by 李煜 (Li Yu, 937–978), the last ruler of the Southern Tang kingdom, remembered today mainly for his beautiful poetry written after its fall.

components.note: 马 (horse) — 骥 names a fine, swift horse.
冀 (jì) gives the sound — an exact match with 骥's reading.

example.hanzi: 他老骥伏枥,仍想为国家做贡献。
example.pinyin: Tā lǎo jì fú lì, réng xiǎng wèi guójiā zuò gòngxiàn.
example.english: Like an old steed still eager to gallop, he still wants to contribute to his country.
example.fact: 老骥伏枥 (lǎo jì fú lì) comes from a poem by the warlord-poet Cao Cao and describes an aging thoroughbred still yearning to run — used today to praise someone old in years but still ambitious.

meanings: the Dai minority living in South China

components.note: 亻 (person) — 傣 names an ethnic group of people.
泰 (tài) gives a sound related to 傣's reading dǎi, sharing the vowel but differing in the initial consonant and tone.

example.hanzi: 傣族主要生活在云南省。
example.pinyin: Dǎizú zhǔyào shēnghuó zài Yúnnán Shěng.
example.english: The Dai ethnic group mainly lives in Yunnan province.
example.fact: The Dai people (傣族) are one of China's 56 officially recognized ethnic groups, concentrated in Yunnan province, and are known for the Water-Splashing Festival that marks their traditional new year.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 嗳 is an interjection and the sound of belching, both mouth-related.
爱 (ài) gives a sound close to 嗳's reading āi, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 嗳,别提了,今天真麻烦。
example.pinyin: Āi, bié tíle, jīntiān zhēn máfan.
example.english: Ugh, don't even mention it, today was really annoying.
example.fact: 嗳 is a "mouth radical" interjection character, part of a family (啊, 呀, 哦, 嗯) built specifically to write spoken exclamations whose only job is to carry tone and emotion, not literal meaning.

components.note: 礻 (spirit/ritual, the 示 radical) — 祯 relates to good omens, traditionally tied to divine favor.
贞 (zhēn) gives the sound — an exact match with 祯's reading.

example.hanzi: 她的名字里有"祯"字,寓意吉祥。
example.pinyin: Tā de míngzi lǐ yǒu "zhēn" zì, yùyì jíxiáng.
example.english: Her name contains the character "祯," symbolizing good fortune.
example.fact: 祯 means "auspicious omen" and, like many characters built on the 礻 (spirit) radical, is popular in given names for the good fortune it is believed to symbolize.

example.hanzi: 酉时大约是下午五点到七点。
example.pinyin: Yǒushí dàyuē shì xiàwǔ wǔ diǎn dào qī diǎn.
example.english: The "you" hour is roughly 5 to 7 in the afternoon.
example.fact: 酉 is a pictograph of a wine jar, and as a radical it appears in nearly every character related to alcohol or fermentation, including 酒 (jiǔ, "wine"), 醒 (xǐng, "to wake up, sober up"), and 醋 (cù, "vinegar").

components.note: 禾 (grain plant) — 秸 names the leftover stalks of a grain crop.
吉 (jí) gives a sound related to 秸's reading jiē, sharing the initial consonant but with the vowel and tone shifted.

example.hanzi: 农民燃烧秸秆会造成空气污染。
example.pinyin: Nóngmín ránshāo jiēgǎn huì zàochéng kōngqì wūrǎn.
example.english: Farmers burning crop stalks can cause air pollution.
example.fact: Burning leftover crop stalks (秸秆焚烧, jiēgǎn fénshāo) after harvest is a major seasonal source of air pollution in parts of rural China, leading to government bans and fines in many provinces.

meanings: to press down heavily with the fingers

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 捺 describes pressing down firmly with the fingers.
奈 (nài) gives a sound close to 捺's reading nà, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 写"人"字的时候,最后一笔是捺。
example.pinyin: Xiě "rén" zì de shíhou, zuìhòu yī bǐ shì nà.
example.english: When writing the character "人," the last stroke is a press-down stroke.
example.fact: 捺 names one of the basic strokes in Chinese calligraphy — the downward-right press stroke — one of just a handful of fundamental strokes (横, 竖, 撇, 捺, 点, etc.) that combine to form every Chinese character.

components.note: 王 (jade) — 瑕 names a flaw specifically in a piece of jade or gem.
叚 (jiǎ) gives a sound related to 瑕's reading xiá, sharing the vowel and tone but with the initial consonant shifted.

example.hanzi: 这件事做得完美无瑕。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì zuò de wánměi wúxiá.
example.english: This matter was done flawlessly.
example.fact: 瑕 originally meant a flaw or spot in jade, and survives today mainly in 完美无瑕 (wánměi wúxiá, "flawless, without blemish") and 瑕疵 (xiácī, "a minor defect").

components.note: 金 (gold) — repeated three times, piling up gold to visually represent great wealth. 鑫 has no traditional etymology beyond this; it was coined for its auspicious look rather than its sound.

example.hanzi: 他的公司叫"鑫鑫贸易"。
example.pinyin: Tā de gōngsī jiào "Xīnxīn Màoyì".
example.english: His company is called "Xinxin Trading."
example.fact: 鑫 was created purely for its lucky appearance — three 金 (gold) stacked together — and is popular in Chinese business and personal names for its association with wealth and prosperity, despite having no real ancient etymology.

components.note: 饣 (eat/food) — 馋 describes an intense craving to eat.

This dataset repeats 饣 as the phonetic element too, which looks like an extraction artifact — 饣 is read shí, not chán. The character's real phonetic/semantic core is likely 毚, the rabbit-shaped component on the right, which reads chán, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 我看到蛋糕就觉得很馋。
example.pinyin: Wǒ kàndào dàngāo jiù juéde hěn chán.
example.english: Seeing the cake makes my mouth water.
example.fact: 馋 describes a craving specifically for food, as in 嘴馋 (zuǐ chán, "to have a sweet tooth"), distinct from general greed (贪), which covers money and other desires.

components.note: 穴 (hole, cave) — 窿 names a cavity or shaft, like a mine shaft.
隆 (lóng) gives the sound — an exact match with 窿's reading.

example.hanzi: 衣服上破了一个窟窿。
example.pinyin: Yīfu shàng pòle yí gè kūlong.
example.english: There's a hole torn in the clothes.
example.fact: 窿 survives almost exclusively in the colloquial word 窟窿 (kūlong), the everyday spoken term for "a hole," while 洞 or 孔 are used more often in written, formal Chinese.

components.note: 木 (wood) — a wedge is typically a wooden tool.
契 (qì) gives a sound now quite distant from 楔's reading xiē — the phonetic connection has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 木匠用楔子把桌子固定住。
example.pinyin: Mùjiang yòng xiēzi bǎ zhuōzi gùdìng zhù.
example.english: The carpenter used a wedge to secure the table.
example.fact: 楔 names a wedge-shaped tool, and lends its shape to 楔形文字 (xiēxíng wénzì, "cuneiform," literally "wedge-shaped writing"), the ancient Mesopotamian writing system.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh/body) — 胱 names a body organ, the bladder.
光 (guāng) gives the sound — an exact match with 胱's reading.

example.hanzi: 膀胱是储存尿液的器官。
example.pinyin: Pángguāng shì chǔcún niàoyè de qìguān.
example.english: The bladder is the organ that stores urine.
example.fact: 胱 appears only in the compound 膀胱 (pángguāng, "bladder"), the organ that stores urine before it is expelled from the body.

components.note: 艹 (grass/plant) — 荔 names a fruit tree, the lychee.
劦 (usually read xié, meaning "united strength") gives a sound now quite distant from 荔's reading lì.

example.hanzi: 荔枝是一种很甜的水果。
example.pinyin: Lìzhī shì yī zhǒng hěn tián de shuǐguǒ.
example.english: Lychee is a very sweet fruit.
example.fact: 荔 appears almost only in 荔枝 (lìzhī, "lychee"). The Song-dynasty poet Su Dongpo loved the fruit so much during his southern exile that he wrote a poem vowing to happily eat three hundred lychees a day.

components.note: 虫 (creature) — 蟆 names a small amphibian, grouped with the 'creature' radical.
莫 (mò) gives a sound related to 蟆's reading má, sharing the initial consonant but with the vowel and tone shifted.

example.hanzi: 池塘里有很多蛤蟆。
example.pinyin: Chítáng lǐ yǒu hěn duō háma.
example.english: There are many frogs and toads in the pond.
example.fact: 蟆 appears almost only in 蛤蟆 (háma), the everyday colloquial word covering both frogs and toads, without the formal distinction that 青蛙 (frog) and 蟾蜍 (toad) make individually.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 湍 describes fast, turbulent water.
耑 (duān) gives a sound close to 湍's reading tuān, differing only in whether the initial consonant is aspirated.

example.hanzi: 河水湍急,很危险。
example.pinyin: Héshuǐ tuānjí, hěn wēixiǎn.
example.english: The river's current is rapid and dangerous.
example.fact: 湍 describes fast-moving water, most often in 湍急 (tuānjí, "turbulent, rapid"), used for dangerous river currents and rapids.

components.note: 山 (mountain) — 屹 describes something standing tall like a mountain.
乞 (qǐ) gives a sound now quite distant from 屹's reading yì — the phonetic link has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 那座山屹立在江边。
example.pinyin: Nà zuò shān yìlì zài jiāngbiān.
example.english: That mountain stands tall by the river.
example.fact: 屹 appears mainly in 屹立 (yìlì, "to stand tall and firm"), often used metaphorically for something standing resolute despite challenges, like a nation or an unwavering person.

components.note: 辶 (walk/movement) — 遐 describes distance one must travel to reach.
叚 (jiǎ) gives a sound related to 遐's reading xiá, sharing the final and tone but with the initial consonant shifted.

example.hanzi: 这位画家名闻遐迩。
example.pinyin: Zhè wèi huàjiā míngwén xiá'ěr.
example.english: This painter is famous far and near.
example.fact: 遐 means "far away" and pairs with its near-opposite 迩 ("near") in the idiom 名闻遐迩 (míngwén xiá'ěr, "famous far and near"), a classical way of saying someone's fame has spread everywhere.

components.note: 车 (cart) — 轲 originally named a part of a cart, an axle.
可 (kě) gives a sound close to 轲's reading kē, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 孟轲,就是孟子,是儒家的代表人物。
example.pinyin: Mèng Kē, jiùshì Mèngzǐ, shì Rújiā de dàibiǎo rénwù.
example.english: Meng Ke, who is Mencius, is a representative figure of Confucianism.
example.fact: 轲 is the given name of 孟子 (Mencius, personal name 孟轲, c. 372–289 BC), the second-most important sage of Confucianism after Confucius himself.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 镯 names a metal bracelet.
蜀 (shǔ) gives a sound now quite distant from 镯's reading zhuó — the phonetic link has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 她手上戴着一个玉镯。
example.pinyin: Tā shǒu shàng dàizhe yí gè yù zhuó.
example.english: She's wearing a jade bracelet on her hand.
example.fact: 镯 names a bracelet, most often seen in 玉镯 (yù zhuó, "jade bracelet"), a traditional piece of jewelry in Chinese culture believed by some to bring good luck or protection to the wearer.

components.note: 纟 (thread/rope) — reins are made of rope or leather strap.
畺 (jiāng) gives the sound — an exact match with 缰's reading.

example.hanzi: 骑手拉紧了马的缰绳。
example.pinyin: Qíshǒu lājǐnle mǎ de jiāngshéng.
example.english: The rider pulled the horse's reins tight.
example.fact: 缰 appears almost only in 缰绳 (jiāngshéng, "reins"), the rope or strap used to control and guide a horse.

components.note: 木 (tree) — 桦 names a type of tree, the birch.
华 (huá) gives a sound close to 桦's reading huà, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 白桦树在东北很常见。
example.pinyin: Báihuà shù zài Dōngběi hěn chángjiàn.
example.english: White birch trees are common in Northeast China.
example.fact: 桦 names the birch tree (白桦, báihuà), common across northern China, Siberia, and Scandinavia, and long valued for its thin, peelable bark, once used as a writing surface.

components.note: 火 (fire) — stewing is a slow-cooking method using heat.
屯 (tún) gives a sound related to 炖's reading dùn, sharing the final but with the initial consonant shifted.

example.hanzi: 妈妈在炖鸡汤。
example.pinyin: Māma zài dùn jītāng.
example.english: Mom is stewing chicken soup.
example.fact: 炖 describes slow-cooking food in liquid over low heat for a long time, the technique behind classic dishes like 炖牛肉 (dùn niúròu, "stewed beef") and many Chinese medicinal soups.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — barium is a metallic element.
贝 (bèi) gives the sound — an exact match with 钡's reading.

example.hanzi: 钡是一种金属元素。
example.pinyin: Bèi shì yī zhǒng jīnshǔ yuánsù.
example.english: Barium is a metallic element.
example.fact: Barium compounds are used in "barium meal" contrast imaging (钡餐), which patients swallow before X-rays so doctors can see the digestive tract clearly.

components.note: 羊 (sheep/goat) — 羚 names an animal in the sheep/goat-like family, the antelope.
令 (lìng) gives a sound close to 羚's reading líng, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 羚羊奔跑的速度非常快。
example.pinyin: Língyáng bēnpǎo de sùdù fēicháng kuài.
example.english: Antelopes run extremely fast.
example.fact: Antelopes (羚羊, língyáng) are among the fastest land animals — the pronghorn, for example, can sustain speeds over 55 km/h to escape predators.

example.hanzi: 他为人很吝啬,从不请客吃饭。
example.pinyin: Tā wéirén hěn lìnsè, cóng bù qǐngkè chīfàn.
example.english: He is very stingy as a person, and never treats others to meals.
example.fact: 啬 means "stingy, miserly," and combines with its near-synonym 吝 to form 吝啬 (lìnsè) — one of the most common ways to call someone stingy in Mandarin.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 诩 describes boasting, an act of speech.
羽 (yǔ) gives a sound close to 诩's reading xǔ, sharing the final and tone but with the initial consonant shifted.

example.hanzi: 他自诩为专家。
example.pinyin: Tā zìxǔ wéi zhuānjiā.
example.english: He boasts of himself as an expert.
example.fact: 诩 appears almost exclusively in 自诩 (zìxǔ), a slightly critical way of saying someone claims a flattering title or quality for themselves, often when others doubt it is deserved.

components.note: 纟 (thread/silk) — 绯 originally described a color of dyed silk.
非 (fēi) gives the sound — an exact match with 绯's reading.

example.hanzi: 记者报道了这起绯闻。
example.pinyin: Jìzhě bàodàole zhè qǐ fēiwén.
example.english: The reporter covered this scandal.
example.fact: 绯 means deep red, but its most common modern use is in 绯闻 (fēiwén, literally "scarlet rumor"), the standard Chinese term for a celebrity's romantic scandal or gossip.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 掖 describes tucking something in with the hands.
夜 (yè) gives a sound close to 掖's reading yē, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 妈妈把被子掖好。
example.pinyin: Māma bǎ bèizi yē hǎo.
example.english: Mom tucked the blanket in snugly.
example.fact: 掖 describes tucking something in with the hands, like tucking in a blanket or hiding something in a pocket or sleeve — a common, everyday gesture verb.

etymologyHint: A bamboo ⺮ record 录; 录 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — the traditional writing material for early Chinese records.
录 (to record) — combined with 'bamboo,' depicts a written record, later specialized to mean a Taoist talisman or register. 录 (lù) is also an exact phonetic match for 箓's reading.

example.hanzi: 道士手里拿着一张符箓。
example.pinyin: Dàoshi shǒu lǐ ná zhe yī zhāng fúlù.
example.english: The Taoist priest holds a talisman in his hand.
example.fact: 箓 refers to a register or talisman in Taoist tradition, most often seen in 符箓 (fúlù), the sacred written charms Daoist priests use in rituals said to command spirits or ward off evil.

etymologyHint: To run out 氵 of strength 固; 固 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 氵 (water) — represents water; 涸 describes water running completely dry.
固 (gù) is credited by tradition as this character's phonetic root, though its modern reading has drifted very far from 涸's hé — a case where the sound link is really only visible historically.

example.hanzi: 由于长期没有下雨,这条河已经干涸了。
example.pinyin: Yóuyú chángqī méiyǒu xiàyǔ, zhè tiáo hé yǐjīng gānhéle.
example.english: Because it hasn't rained for a long time, this river has already dried up.
example.fact: 涸 appears mainly in 干涸 (gānhé, "dried up, parched"), commonly used for rivers, lakes, or wells that have run completely dry, often due to drought.

components.note: 鸟 (bird) — 鸳 names a waterbird, the male mandarin duck.
夗 (yuàn) gives a sound close to 鸳's reading yuān, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 鸳鸯是一种美丽的水鸟。
example.pinyin: Yuānyāng shì yī zhǒng měilì de shuǐniǎo.
example.english: Mandarin ducks are a kind of beautiful waterbird.
example.fact: 鸳鸯 (yuānyāng, "mandarin ducks") are a classic symbol of marital devotion in Chinese culture, since the male (鸳) and female (鸯) are traditionally believed to always appear together in pairs.

components.note: 土 (earth) — 塾 relates to a physical place, a schoolhouse.
孰 (shú) gives the sound — an exact match with 塾's reading.

example.hanzi: 私塾是古代的私人学校。
example.pinyin: Sīshú shì gǔdài de sīrén xuéxiào.
example.english: A private academy was a private school in ancient times.
example.fact: 塾 names a traditional private school, best known in 私塾 (sīshú), the small tutoring academies where Chinese children studied the Confucian classics before public schools became common in the 20th century.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 呸 is an interjection expressing contempt through the mouth, like spitting.
丕 (pī) gives a sound related to 呸's reading pēi, sharing the initial and tone but with the vowel shifted.

example.hanzi: 呸!你说的都是假话!
example.pinyin: Pēi! Nǐ shuō de dōu shì jiǎhuà!
example.english: Pah! Everything you said is lies!
example.fact: 呸 is a pure interjection imitating the sound of spitting in contempt or disgust, used much like "pah!" or "bah!" in English — it carries no meaning beyond the emotional reaction itself.

meanings: to swing (one's arms, a heavy object)

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 抡 describes swinging something with the arm.
仑 (lún) gives a sound close to 抡's reading lūn, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他抡起斧头砍树。
example.pinyin: Tā lūn qǐ fǔtou kǎn shù.
example.english: He swung the axe up to chop the tree.
example.fact: 抡 describes swinging something heavy through a wide arc of the arm, typically a tool or weapon like an axe, hammer, or bat.

meanings: used in 抖擻|抖擞[dou3 sou3]
(dialect) to stoke the embers (to revive a fire)

components.note: 扌 (hand) — many senses of 擞 involve a shaking or rousing action.
数 (shù) gives a sound now quite distant from 擞's reading sǒu — the phonetic link has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 他精神抖擞地走进了教室。
example.pinyin: Tā jīngshén dǒusǒu de zǒu jìnle jiàoshì.
example.english: He walked into the classroom full of energy and spirit.
example.fact: 擞 survives almost only in the idiom 精神抖擞 (jīngshén dǒusǒu, "full of vigor and spirit"), a common phrase for looking energetic and lively.

components.note: 灬 (fire) — 熹 describes warmth and glimmering light.
喜 (xǐ) gives a sound close to 熹's reading xī, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 朱熹是宋代著名的哲学家。
example.pinyin: Zhū Xī shì Sòngdài zhùmíng de zhéxuéjiā.
example.english: Zhu Xi was a famous philosopher of the Song dynasty.
example.fact: 熹 is best known as part of the name of 朱熹 (Zhu Xi, 1130–1200), the influential Song-dynasty philosopher whose Neo-Confucian interpretations shaped Chinese and East Asian thought for centuries.

components.note: 土 (earth) — 坷 names a clod or lump of earth.
可 (kě) gives the sound — an exact match with 坷's reading.

example.hanzi: 他的一生非常坎坷。
example.pinyin: Tā de yīshēng fēicháng kǎnkě.
example.english: His life was extremely bumpy and full of hardship.
example.fact: 坷 appears mainly in 坎坷 (kǎnkě), literally describing rough, bumpy terrain but almost always used figuratively today for a difficult, hardship-filled life or path.

meanings: pottery container for water, wine etc

components.note: 瓦 (tile/pottery) — 瓮 names a large pottery jar.
公 (gōng) gives a sound now quite distant from 瓮's reading wèng — the phonetic link has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 他用请君入瓮的办法让对方说出了实话。
example.pinyin: Tā yòng qǐng jūn rù wèng de bànfǎ ràng duìfāng shuō chūle shíhuà.
example.english: He used the "invite you into the jar" trick to get the other person to tell the truth.
example.fact: 请君入瓮 (qǐng jūn rù wèng, literally "please get into the jar, sir") comes from a Tang-dynasty legal anecdote about an interrogator who unwittingly described his own torture method to the very official investigating him — now used for someone trapped by their own trick.

etymologyHint: Stretching from heaven 一 to earth 一

components.note: 一 (a horizontal line, appearing twice, above and below the center) — depicts something extending steadily from one boundary to another, giving 亘 its meaning "to stretch across, extend throughout."

example.hanzi: 这个传统亘古不变。
example.pinyin: Zhège chuántǒng gèngǔ bùbiàn.
example.english: This tradition has remained unchanged since ancient times.
example.fact: 亘 appears mainly in 亘古 (gèngǔ, "since time immemorial"), a literary way of emphasizing that something has existed continuously throughout all of history.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 嗟 describes a sigh, made through the mouth.
差 gives a sound now quite distant from 嗟's reading jiē — the phonetic link has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 他宁死不食嗟来之食。
example.pinyin: Tā nìngsǐ bù shí jiēláizhīshí.
example.english: He would rather die than eat food given to him with contempt.
example.fact: 嗟来之食 (jiēláizhīshí) comes from an ancient story of a starving man who refused food offered scornfully, insisting he would rather die than accept charity given without respect.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — 筵 originally named a bamboo mat spread on the floor.
延 (yán) gives the sound — an exact match with 筵's reading.

example.hanzi: 婚礼上摆了几十桌筵席。
example.pinyin: Hūnlǐ shàng bǎile jǐshí zhuō yánxí.
example.english: Dozens of banquet tables were set up at the wedding.
example.fact: 筵 originally meant a bamboo mat spread on the floor for sitting, and by extension came to mean the banquet held on it, surviving today in 筵席 (yánxí, "banquet feast").

components.note: 足 (foot) — 跛 describes a limp, a foot-related impairment.
皮 (pí) gives a sound now fairly distant from 跛's reading bǒ, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 他因为受伤走路有点跛。
example.pinyin: Tā yīnwèi shòushāng zǒulù yǒudiǎn bǒ.
example.english: Because of his injury, he walks with a bit of a limp.
example.fact: 跛 describes a limp or lameness, most often in 一瘸一跛 (yī qué yī bǒ), a vivid four-character phrase for someone limping unevenly with each step.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 汕 originally named a bamboo fish trap used in water.
山 (shān) gives a sound close to 汕's reading shàn, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 汕头是广东省的一个海滨城市。
example.pinyin: Shàntóu shì Guǎngdōng Shěng de yí gè hǎibīn chéngshì.
example.english: Shantou is a coastal city in Guangdong province.
example.fact: 汕 today survives mainly in the place name 汕头 (Shàntóu), a coastal city in Guangdong that was one of China's earliest treaty ports opened to foreign trade in the 19th century.

meanings: a final particle used to express admiration

components.note: 欠 (to lack, to owe; also a mouth-open shape) — used in several particle/exclamation characters.
与 (yú) gives the sound — an exact match with 欤's reading.

example.hanzi: 此非君子之道欤?
example.pinyin: Cǐ fēi jūnzǐ zhī dào yú?
example.english: Is this not the way of a gentleman?
example.fact: 欤 is a Classical Chinese question particle, equivalent to modern 吗 or 呢, and essentially never appears in contemporary spoken or written Mandarin outside of quoting classical texts.

etymologyHint: A ditch 㕡 carved in the earth 土; 㕡 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 土 (earth) — represents earth; 壑 names a ravine carved into the ground.
㕡 depicts a ditch or hollow; combined with 'earth,' forms the image of a deep gully. 㕡 also traditionally supplied 壑's pronunciation, though the modern reading hè has drifted from it.

example.hanzi: 他贪得无厌,真是欲壑难填。
example.pinyin: Tā tān dé wúyàn, zhēnshi yù hè nán tián.
example.english: He is so greedy — truly a bottomless pit of desire.
example.fact: 壑 names a deep ravine, and the idiom 欲壑难填 (yù hè nán tián, "a ravine of desire that's hard to fill") vividly compares insatiable greed to a gorge that can never be filled up.

components.note: 水 (water) — 颍 names a river.

example.hanzi: 颍河是淮河的支流。
example.pinyin: Yǐng Hé shì Huái Hé de zhīliú.
example.english: The Ying River is a tributary of the Huai River.
example.fact: 颍 names the Ying River (颍河), a major tributary of the Huai River flowing through Henan and Anhui provinces — the character survives today mainly in this river name and as a surname.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 溥's original meaning 'vast, widespread' was likened to a great expanse of water.
尃 (fū) gives a sound now quite distant from 溥's reading pǔ — the phonetic link has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 溥仪是中国最后一位皇帝。
example.pinyin: Pǔyí shì Zhōngguó zuìhòu yī wèi huángdì.
example.english: Puyi was the last emperor of China.
example.fact: 溥 is best known as part of the name of 溥仪 (Puyi, 1906–1967), the last emperor of the Qing dynasty, who ascended the throne as a small child and later lived to see China become a republic.

meanings: used in 姍姍|姗姗[shan1 shan1]

components.note: 女 (woman) — 姗's original sense described a woman's graceful, slow gait.
册 (cè) gives a sound now quite distant from 姗's reading shān — the phonetic link has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 她姗姗来迟。
example.pinyin: Tā shānshān lái chí.
example.english: She arrived fashionably late.
example.fact: 姗 survives almost only in the idiom 姗姗来迟 (shānshān láichí, "to arrive slowly and late"), originally describing a graceful, leisurely gait, now used for anyone who shows up later than expected.

components.note: 足 (foot) — 踊 describes leaping, a foot-powered action.
甬 (yǒng) gives the sound — an exact match with 踊's reading.

example.hanzi: 大家踊跃参加这次活动。
example.pinyin: Dàjiā yǒngyuè cānjiā zhè cì huódòng.
example.english: Everyone eagerly took part in this activity.
example.fact: 踊 survives mainly in 踊跃 (yǒngyuè), literally "to leap up," now used figuratively to describe eager, enthusiastic participation, as in 踊跃发言 ("to eagerly speak up").

etymologyHint: A bird 鸟 roosting in a tree 木

components.note: 鸟 (bird) — represents a bird, specifically an owl.
木 (tree) — combined with 'bird,' depicts an owl perched in a tree. 枭 later extended to mean a fierce, cunning figure, as in 毒枭 (dúxiāo, "drug kingpin").

example.hanzi: 警方抓住了这个毒枭。
example.pinyin: Jǐngfāng zhuāzhùle zhège dúxiāo.
example.english: The police caught this drug kingpin.
example.fact: 枭 originally meant "owl" but by extension now names a ruthless, powerful criminal boss, most commonly in 毒枭 (dúxiāo, "drug lord"), a term frequently seen in Chinese news and crime dramas.

components.note: 日 (sun) — 暄 originally described warmth from sunlight.
宣 (xuān) gives the sound — an exact match with 暄's reading.

example.hanzi: 见面时,他们先寒暄了几句。
example.pinyin: Jiànmiàn shí, tāmen xiān hánxuānle jǐ jù.
example.english: When they met, they first exchanged a few pleasantries.
example.fact: 暄 appears mainly in 寒暄 (hánxuān), the standard word for exchanging small talk (literally "cold and warm"), referencing the classic opening topic of commenting on the weather.

meanings: God of cereals worshiped by ancient rulers

components.note: 禾 (grain plant) — 稷 originally named a type of millet and the god associated with grain harvests.
畟 gives a sound now quite distant from 稷's reading jì — the phonetic link has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 古人常用"社稷"来指代国家。
example.pinyin: Gǔrén cháng yòng "shèjì" lái zhǐdài guójiā.
example.english: Ancient people often used "sheji" to refer to the state.
example.fact: 稷 was the god of grain in ancient Chinese belief, and paired with 社 (the god of soil) to form 社稷 (shèjì), a classical term for "the state" — since a stable nation depended on its land and its harvests.

meanings: used in 蹣跚|蹒跚[pan2 shan1]

components.note: 足 (foot) — 跚 describes an unsteady walking gait.
册 (cè) gives a sound now quite distant from 跚's reading shān — the phonetic link has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 他步履蹒跚地走了过来。
example.pinyin: Tā bùlǚ pánshān de zǒule guòlái.
example.english: He walked over with a staggering, unsteady gait.
example.fact: 跚 appears almost only in 蹒跚 (pánshān), a word describing an unsteady, wobbling gait — often used for the very young, the very old, or the injured.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 涟 describes ripples on water.
连 (lián) gives the sound — an exact match with 涟's reading.

example.hanzi: 湖面上泛起了一圈涟漪。
example.pinyin: Húmiàn shàng fànqǐle yī quān liányī.
example.english: Ripples spread across the lake's surface.
example.fact: 涟 names gentle ripples on water, as in 涟漪 (liányī), a word often used poetically for the small emotional "ripples" a memory or event leaves behind, similar to the English "ripple effect."

components.note: 氵 (water) — 瀛 names a large body of water, the sea.
嬴 (yíng) gives the sound — an exact match with 瀛's reading.

example.hanzi: 东瀛是对日本的一种古称。
example.pinyin: Dōngyíng shì duì Rìběn de yī zhǒng gǔchēng.
example.english: "Dongying" is an old poetic name for Japan.
example.fact: 瀛 means "sea, ocean" and appears in 东瀛 (dōngyíng, literally "eastern seas"), a poetic classical name for Japan still used today in more literary or nostalgic contexts.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — the sheng is made of bamboo pipes.
生 (shēng) gives the sound — an exact match with 笙's reading.

example.hanzi: 笙是一种古老的中国乐器。
example.pinyin: Shēng shì yī zhǒng gǔlǎo de Zhōngguó yuèqì.
example.english: The sheng is an ancient Chinese musical instrument.
example.fact: 笙 (the sheng) is a free-reed mouth organ made of bamboo pipes, one of the oldest Chinese instruments, and its reed mechanism is believed to have influenced the design of the European harmonica and accordion.

meanings: an ancient state in Shandong province
vassal state of Zhou in Shandong

example.hanzi: 滕王阁是江西南昌的一座名楼。
example.pinyin: Téngwáng Gé shì Jiāngxī Nánchāng de yī zuò mínglóu.
example.english: Tengwang Pavilion is a famous tower in Nanchang, Jiangxi.
example.fact: 滕 survives today mainly in 滕王阁 (Tengwang Pavilion) in Nanchang, made famous by the Tang-dynasty writer Wang Bo's essay "滕王阁序," one of the most celebrated pieces of classical Chinese prose, still memorized by students today.

components.note: 足 (foot) — the ankle is part of the foot and leg joint system.
果 (guǒ) gives a sound now quite distant from 踝's reading huái — the phonetic link has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 他跑步的时候扭伤了踝关节。
example.pinyin: Tā pǎobù de shíhou niǔshāngle huái guānjié.
example.english: He sprained his ankle while running.
example.fact: 踝 names the ankle joint, most often seen in 脚踝 (jiǎohuái, "ankle") — one of the most commonly sprained joints in the body due to the sideways stress it takes during runs, jumps, and uneven steps.

etymologyHint: A banker's 贝 two 二 with accents to prevent forgery

components.note: 二 (two) — represents the number two.

贝 (money/shell) — combined with 'two,' forms an elaborate, hard-to-forge way of writing '2' for financial documents, much like spelling out "two" instead of writing "2" to prevent alteration on a check.

example.hanzi: 这张支票上的金额是贰佰元。
example.pinyin: Zhè zhāng zhīpiào shàng de jīn'é shì èrbǎi yuán.
example.english: The amount on this check is two hundred yuan.
example.fact: 贰 is one of a special set of "banker's numerals" (壹, 贰, 叁, 肆...) used on checks, contracts, and financial documents in place of 一二三四, precisely because the ordinary numerals are too easy to alter or forge by adding a stroke.

meanings: to look down from a height

components.note: 目 (eye) — 瞰 describes looking down from a height.
敢 (gǎn) gives a sound related to 瞰's reading kàn, sharing the initial's place of articulation and the final, but differing in tone.

example.hanzi: 从山顶可以俯瞰整个城市。
example.pinyin: Cóng shāndǐng kěyǐ fǔkàn zhěnggè chéngshì.
example.english: From the mountaintop you can look down over the whole city.
example.fact: 瞰 appears mainly in 俯瞰 (fǔkàn, "to look down from above") and 鸟瞰 (niǎokàn, "bird's-eye view"), both describing the vantage point of looking down from a height.

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 恻 describes an emotional feeling, compassion or anguish.
则 (zé) gives a sound related to 恻's reading cè, sharing the vowel but with the initial consonant and tone shifted.

example.hanzi: 看到那只受伤的小狗,他心生恻隐之心。
example.pinyin: Kàndào nà zhī shòushāng de xiǎogǒu, tā xīn shēng cèyǐn zhī xīn.
example.english: Seeing that injured puppy, he felt a compassionate stirring in his heart.
example.fact: 恻隐之心 (cèyǐn zhī xīn, "a heart of compassion") comes from Mencius, who argued that this instinctive pity for others' suffering is proof that human nature is fundamentally good.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — a sneeze is expelled through the mouth and nose.
疐 (zhì) gives a sound related to 嚏's reading tì, sharing the final and tone but with the initial consonant shifted.

example.hanzi: 他感冒了,一直打喷嚏。
example.pinyin: Tā gǎnmàole, yīzhí dǎ pēntì.
example.english: He caught a cold and keeps sneezing.
example.fact: 嚏 appears only inside 打喷嚏 (dǎ pēntì, "to sneeze") — a sneeze can expel droplets at surprising speed and over a distance of several meters, making it one of the body's most forceful reflexes.

components.note: 辶 (walk/movement) — 迢 describes distance covered on a journey.
召 (zhào) gives a sound now quite distant from 迢's reading tiáo — the phonetic link has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 他千里迢迢地来看我。
example.pinyin: Tā qiānlǐ tiáotiáo de lái kàn wǒ.
example.english: He traveled a thousand miles to come see me.
example.fact: 迢 appears mainly in 千里迢迢 (qiānlǐ tiáotiáo), a vivid four-character phrase emphasizing that someone traveled a great distance, often used to highlight the effort or sincerity behind a visit.

components.note: 犭 (dog/beast) — 獗 describes wild, unchecked behavior, likened to an unruly animal.
厥 (jué) gives the sound — an exact match with 獗's reading.

example.hanzi: 那个地区的犯罪活动十分猖獗。
example.pinyin: Nàge dìqū de fànzuì huódòng shífēn chāngjué.
example.english: Criminal activity is extremely rampant in that area.
example.fact: 獗 exists only in 猖獗 (chāngjué), a word for something running unchecked and out of control, commonly used for crime, disease outbreaks, or corruption.

components.note: 阝 (a place/settlement) — 邯 names a city.
甘 (gān) gives a sound close to 邯's reading hán, sharing the final but with the initial consonant shifted.

example.hanzi: 他学别人的样子,结果邯郸学步,什么都不会了。
example.pinyin: Tā xué biérén de yàngzi, jiéguǒ Hándān xué bù, shénme dōu bù huìle.
example.english: He copied others' style, and ended up like the man of Handan learning to walk — forgetting how to do anything at all.
example.fact: 邯郸学步 (Hándān xué bù) comes from a Zhuangzi story about a man who went to the city of Handan to learn its elegant local gait, but only ended up forgetting how to walk at all — the classic idiom for blindly imitating others.

components.note: 目 (eye) — 睑 names a part of the eye, the eyelid.
佥 (qiān) gives a sound now quite distant from 睑's reading jiǎn — the phonetic link has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 他的眼睑有点红肿。
example.pinyin: Tā de yǎnjiǎn yǒudiǎn hóngzhǒng.
example.english: His eyelid is a bit red and swollen.
example.fact: 睑 appears almost only in the medical/formal term 眼睑 (yǎnjiǎn, "eyelid"), while everyday speech more often just says 眼皮 (yǎnpí).

components.note: 贝 (money) — 赡 relates to financially supporting someone.
詹 (zhān) gives a sound now quite distant from 赡's reading shàn — the phonetic link has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 子女有赡养父母的义务。
example.pinyin: Zǐnǚ yǒu shànyǎng fùmǔ de yìwù.
example.english: Children have the duty to support their parents.
example.fact: 赡 appears mainly in 赡养 (shànyǎng, "to support financially," especially elderly parents), a legal duty explicitly written into China's marriage and civil law.

components.note: 糸 (silk thread) — 萦 describes something coiling or winding, like thread wrapping around itself.

example.hanzi: 这段音乐一直萦绕在我耳边。
example.pinyin: Zhè duàn yīnyuè yīzhí yíngrào zài wǒ ěrbiān.
example.english: This piece of music keeps lingering in my ears.
example.fact: 萦 usually appears in 萦绕 (yíngrào), a poetic word for something that lingers persistently, such as a memory, melody, or scent that keeps "coiling around" one's mind.

etymologyHint: An ear 耳 ring 王; 耳 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 王 (jade) — represents jade; 珥 names a jade or pearl earring.
耳 (ear) — combined with 'jade,' depicts a jade ornament worn at the ear. 耳 (ěr) is also an exact phonetic match for 珥's reading.

example.hanzi: 古代女子常佩戴玉珥作为装饰。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài nǚzǐ cháng pèidài yù ěr zuòwéi zhuāngshì.
example.english: Ancient women often wore jade earrings as decoration.
example.fact: 珥 is a classical word for an ear ornament, typically jade or pearl, worn by aristocratic women in ancient China as both decoration and a sign of status.

components.note: 酉 (a wine vessel, used as the chemistry radical) — 酮 names a class of organic compounds, ketones.
同 (tóng) gives the sound — an exact match with 酮's reading.

example.hanzi: 丙酮是一种常见的有机溶剂。
example.pinyin: Bǐngtóng shì yī zhǒng chángjiàn de yǒujī róngjì.
example.english: Acetone is a common organic solvent.
example.fact: 酮 names the ketone functional group in chemistry, seen in words like 丙酮 (bǐngtóng, "acetone"), the solvent found in nail polish remover.

components.note: 王 (jade) — 璞 names an unpolished, uncarved piece of jade.
菐 (pú) gives the sound — an exact match with 璞's reading.

example.hanzi: 他是一块未经雕琢的璞玉。
example.pinyin: Tā shì yī kuài wèi jīng diāozhuó de púyù.
example.english: He is an uncut piece of jade (raw, unrefined talent).
example.fact: 璞玉 (púyù, "uncut jade") is a common metaphor in Chinese for raw, unrefined potential or talent that hasn't yet been shaped or polished into its full value.

etymologyHint: A pleasing 美 lamb 羔 soup

components.note: 羔 (lamb) — ancient soups were often made from lamb or mutton.

美 (pleasing, delicious) — combined with 'lamb,' conveys a delicious soup or broth. 美 itself is thought to originally depict a large, fattened sheep — beauty and deliciousness sharing the same sheep-based root.

example.hanzi: 这碗鸡蛋羹很好吃。
example.pinyin: Zhè wǎn jīdàn gēng hěn hǎochī.
example.english: This bowl of steamed egg custard is delicious.
example.fact: 羹 names a thick soup or custard-like dish, as in 鸡蛋羹 (jīdàn gēng, "steamed egg custard"), a popular home-style Chinese dish with a silky, pudding-like texture.

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 缄 originally meant to seal or bind something shut, like tying a letter closed.
咸 (xián) gives a sound related to 缄's reading jiān, sharing the final but with the initial consonant and tone shifted.

example.hanzi: 面对记者的提问,他选择缄默。
example.pinyin: Miànduì jìzhě de tíwèn, tā xuǎnzé jiānmò.
example.english: Faced with the reporter's questions, he chose to remain silent.
example.fact: 缄 originally meant to seal or bind shut, like sealing a letter, and this idea of being "sealed" extended metaphorically to 缄默 (jiānmò), meaning to stay tight-lipped and silent.

components.note: 日 (sun) — 晾 describes drying something by exposing it to sunlight or air.
京 (jīng) gives a sound now quite distant from 晾's reading liàng — the phonetic link has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 妈妈把衣服晾在阳台上。
example.pinyin: Māma bǎ yīfu liàng zài yángtái shàng.
example.english: Mom hung the clothes to dry on the balcony.
example.fact: 晾 describes drying something in the sun or air, as in 晾衣服 (liàng yīfu, "to hang laundry to dry"), and figuratively means to leave someone waiting or ignored, as in 把他晾在一边 ("to leave him out in the cold").

etymologyHint: Wages offered 奉 to a person 亻; 奉 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 亻 (person) — represents a person, the recipient of wages.
奉 (to offer respectfully) — combined with 'person,' depicts wages given to an official. 奉 (fèng) is also an exact phonetic match for 俸's reading.

example.hanzi: 古代官员的俸禄由国家发放。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài guānyuán de fènglù yóu guójiā fāfàng.
example.english: Ancient officials' salaries were paid by the state.
example.fact: 俸 names an official's salary, most often in 俸禄 (fènglù), the historical term for the stipend paid to government officials in imperial China, sometimes in cash but often partly in grain.

components.note: 女 (woman) — 媲's original meaning involved marrying a woman as an equal match, later extended to 'comparable to.'

example.hanzi: 这座城市的夜景可以媲美纽约。
example.pinyin: Zhè zuò chéngshì de yèjǐng kěyǐ pìměi Niǔyuē.
example.english: This city's night view can rival New York's.
example.fact: 媲 survives mainly in 媲美 (pìměi), a word for being comparable to or rivaling something else in quality or beauty, often used to praise something as being "on par with" a world-famous standard.

components.note: 鸟 (bird) — 鸾 names a mythical bird. This dataset lists 亦 as semantic and 鸟 as phonetic, which looks reversed from the obvious meaning — 鸟 (bird) is clearly the semantic element here.
亦's link to 鸾's reading luán is unclear; this looks like a labeling artifact from the simplified glyph's shape rather than a genuine phonetic clue.

example.hanzi: 古代传说中,鸾是一种像凤凰的神鸟。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài chuánshuō zhōng, luán shì yī zhǒng xiàng fènghuáng de shénniǎo.
example.english: In ancient legend, the luan was a divine bird resembling the phoenix.
example.fact: 鸾 names a mythical bird closely associated with the phoenix (凤) in Chinese legend, and the pairing 鸾凤 is a classical symbol for a blissfully matched husband and wife.

meanings: used in 慫恿|怂恿[song3 yong3]

components.note: 心 (heart) — 恿 relates to inner urging or incitement.
甬 (yǒng) gives the sound — an exact match with 恿's reading.

example.hanzi: 朋友怂恿他去做那件危险的事。
example.pinyin: Péngyou sǒngyǒng tā qù zuò nà jiàn wēixiǎn de shì.
example.english: His friend egged him on to do that dangerous thing.
example.fact: 恿 appears only inside 怂恿 (sǒngyǒng, "to incite, to egg someone on"), a word that always carries a negative connotation of encouraging someone toward a bad or risky decision.

etymologyHint: Crooked 宛 like an insect 虫; 宛 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 虫 (insect) — represents a small creature; describes something moving or curving like an insect or snake.
宛 (winding, curved) — combined with 'insect,' gives 蜿 its meaning of twisting and winding, as in 蜿蜒 (wānyán, "to meander"). 宛 (wǎn) is also very close to 蜿's reading wān, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 这条小路蜿蜒地伸向山顶。
example.pinyin: Zhè tiáo xiǎolù wānyán de shēnxiàng shāndǐng.
example.english: This small path winds its way up to the mountaintop.
example.fact: 蜿 appears almost only in 蜿蜒 (wānyán), a word for something winding and twisting like a snake, commonly used to describe mountain roads, rivers, and the Great Wall of China.

etymologyHint: To sacrifice 卖 a calf 牛

components.note: 牛 (cow/ox) — represents cattle; 犊 names a calf, a young cow.

卖, here representing an old sense unrelated to its modern meaning 'to sell,' combines with 'cow' to depict a calf offered as a sacrifice; it is also the traditional phonetic root, though its modern reading has drifted from 犊's dú.

example.hanzi: 他就像初生牛犊,什么都不怕。
example.pinyin: Tā jiù xiàng chūshēng niúdú, shénme dōu bùpà.
example.english: He's like a newborn calf, afraid of nothing.
example.fact: 犊 appears mainly in the idiom 初生牛犊不怕虎 ("a newborn calf isn't afraid of a tiger"), used to describe someone young and inexperienced who acts fearlessly, not yet knowing enough to be afraid.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 讷 describes being slow or clumsy with words.
内 (nèi) gives a sound close to 讷's reading nè, sharing the initial consonant but with the vowel shifted.

example.hanzi: 他性格木讷,不太会说话。
example.pinyin: Tā xìnggé mùnè, bù tài huì shuōhuà.
example.english: He has an awkward, inarticulate personality and isn't great with words.
example.fact: 讷 describes being slow or clumsy with words, most often in 木讷 (mùnè) — notably, this trait was actually praised by Confucius, who said in the Analects that the firm, resolute, and inarticulate are close to true virtue.

components.note: 邑 (city/settlement) — 扈's original sense involved a retinue or escort tied to a place.
户 (hù) gives the sound — an exact match with 扈's reading.

example.hanzi: 他为人飞扬跋扈,不把别人放在眼里。
example.pinyin: Tā wéirén fēiyáng báhù, bù bǎ biérén fàngzài yǎnlǐ.
example.english: He acts arrogant and domineering, looking down on everyone else.
example.fact: 扈 appears mainly in 跋扈 (báhù) and the idiom 飞扬跋扈 (fēiyáng báhù), describing someone who is domineering and acts as though above the rules.

components.note: 虫 (insect/creature) — 蜈 names a many-legged creature, the centipede.
吴 (wú) gives the sound — an exact match with 蜈's reading.

example.hanzi: 蜈蚣有很多只脚。
example.pinyin: Wúgōng yǒu hěn duō zhī jiǎo.
example.english: Centipedes have many legs.
example.fact: Despite their name ("hundred legs" in both English and 蜈蚣's Chinese origin), most centipede species actually have far fewer than 100 legs, while some have over 300 — the count is always an odd pair per body segment, never a perfect hundred.

etymologyHint: A bird 隹 with a plumed 羽 tail

components.note: 隹 (a short-tailed bird) — represents a bird.
羽 (feather) — combined with 'bird,' depicts a long-tailed, plumed pheasant.

example.hanzi: 翟是一个比较少见的姓氏。
example.pinyin: Zhái shì yī gè bǐjiào shǎojiàn de xìngshì.
example.english: Zhai is a relatively uncommon surname.
example.fact: 翟 has two readings depending on use — dí when it means "pheasant, plumes" in classical texts, and zhái when used as a surname, a pattern seen in several Chinese characters whose reading shifts specifically for names.

components.note: 艹 (plant) — 藕 names an aquatic plant's edible root.
耦 (ǒu) gives the sound — an exact match with 藕's reading.

example.hanzi: 藕是一种可以吃的水生植物根茎。
example.pinyin: Ǒu shì yī zhǒng kěyǐ chī de shuǐshēng zhíwù gēnjīng.
example.english: Lotus root is an edible aquatic plant rhizome.
example.fact: 藕 (lotus root) has a distinctive lattice of holes running through its cross-section, and the idiom 藕断丝连 ("the lotus root breaks but the fibers stay connected") describes a relationship that seems ended but still has lingering emotional ties.

meanings: used in 屈戌兒|屈戌儿[qu1 qu5 r5]

example.hanzi: 1898年的"戊戌变法"是中国近代史上的重要事件。
example.pinyin: Yī bā jiǔ bā nián de "Wùxū Biànfǎ" shì Zhōngguó jìndàishǐ shàng de zhòngyào shìjiàn.
example.english: The "Wuxu Reform" of 1898 was an important event in modern Chinese history.
example.fact: 戌 is the 11th of the 12 Earthly Branches, tied to the Year of the Dog, and gives its name to 戊戌变法, a famous failed attempt to modernize the Qing dynasty in 1898.

components.note: 艹 (plant) — 蓓 describes a flower bud.
倍 (bèi) gives the sound — an exact match with 蓓's reading.

example.hanzi: 花园里的花蓓蕾初绽。
example.pinyin: Huāyuán lǐ de huā bèilěi chūzhàn.
example.english: The flower buds in the garden are just beginning to open.
example.fact: 蓓 appears almost only in 蓓蕾 (bèilěi), a poetic word for a flower bud not yet in bloom, often used metaphorically for youthful promise or something just beginning to develop.

example.hanzi: 他的名字里有一个"鋆"字。
example.pinyin: Tā de míngzi lǐ yǒu yí gè "yún" zì.
example.english: His name contains the character "鋆."
example.fact: 鋆 means "gold" but has almost no use in ordinary vocabulary — like 鑫, it exists mainly as an auspicious-sounding, wealth-themed character chosen for personal names rather than for everyday communication.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 谩 describes verbal abuse or deception.
曼 (màn) gives a sound close to 谩's reading mán, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 网络上谩骂他人是不文明的行为。
example.pinyin: Wǎngluò shàng mànmà tārén shì bù wénmíng de xíngwéi.
example.english: Insulting others online is an uncivil behavior.
example.fact: 谩 appears mainly in 谩骂 (mànmà), meaning to hurl abuse or insults, a word frequently used to describe toxic behavior in online comment sections.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 谀 describes flattery, an act of speech.
臾 (yú) gives the sound — an exact match with 谀's reading.

example.hanzi: 他经常阿谀奉承领导。
example.pinyin: Tā jīngcháng āyú fèngchéng lǐngdǎo.
example.english: He often flatters his boss obsequiously.
example.fact: 谀 appears mainly in the idiom 阿谀奉承 (āyú fèngchéng), a four-character phrase for shameless flattery and sycophancy toward someone in a position of power.

meanings: mortise (slot cut into wood to receive a tenon)

example.hanzi: 他卯足了劲准备这次考试。
example.pinyin: Tā mǎozúle jìn zhǔnbèi zhè cì kǎoshì.
example.english: He mustered all his strength preparing for this exam.
example.fact: 卯 is the 4th of the 12 Earthly Branches, tied to the Year of the Rabbit, and survives in modern slang as 卯足劲 (mǎozú jìn), meaning to gather and focus all one's energy toward a goal.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 谙 describes verbal familiarity and fluency.
音 (yīn) gives a sound now quite distant from 谙's reading ān — the phonetic link has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 他年纪还小,不谙世事。
example.pinyin: Tā niánjì hái xiǎo, bù ān shìshì.
example.english: He is still young and not yet worldly-wise.
example.fact: 谙 appears mainly in phrases like 不谙世事 (bù ān shìshì, "unfamiliar with the ways of the world"), typically describing someone naive due to youth or inexperience.

components.note: 山 (mountain) — 岐 describes something high and majestic, like a mountain.
支 (zhī) gives a sound now quite distant from 岐's reading qí — the phonetic link has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 岐山是周朝发源地之一。
example.pinyin: Qíshān shì Zhōucháo fāyuándì zhī yī.
example.english: Mount Qi is one of the birthplaces of the Zhou dynasty.
example.fact: 岐 names Mount Qi (岐山) in Shaanxi province, traditionally considered one of the cradles of the Zhou dynasty (1046–256 BC), one of the longest-lasting dynasties in Chinese history.

components.note: 虫 (creature) — 蝎 names a small venomous creature, the scorpion.
曷 (hé) gives a sound now quite distant from 蝎's reading xiē — the phonetic link has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 蝎子有毒,要小心。
example.pinyin: Xiēzi yǒudú, yào xiǎoxīn.
example.english: Scorpions are venomous, so be careful.
example.fact: Scorpions (蝎子) have existed for over 400 million years, making them one of the oldest surviving animal groups on Earth, largely unchanged since before the age of dinosaurs.

components.note: 艹 (plant) — 荼 originally named a bitter herb.
余 (yú) gives a sound now quite distant from 荼's reading tú — the phonetic link has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 这场比赛正如火如荼地进行着。
example.pinyin: Zhè chǎng bǐsài zhèng rúhuǒrútú de jìnxíngzhe.
example.english: This competition is currently in full, intense swing.
example.fact: 荼 originally named a bitter herb whose white flowers were compared to fire in the idiom 如火如荼 (rúhuǒrútú, "like fire and like [white] flowers"), now used for anything happening at full, blazing intensity.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 镀 describes coating something with a metal layer.
度 (dù) gives the sound — an exact match with 镀's reading.

example.hanzi: 这个戒指镀了一层金。
example.pinyin: Zhège jièzhi dùle yī céng jīn.
example.english: This ring is plated with a layer of gold.
example.fact: 镀 describes coating a surface with a thin metal layer, as in 镀金 (dùjīn, "gold-plated") — the same idea behind the English phrase "gold-plated," for something that looks valuable but is only superficially so.

components.note: 木 (tree) — 椰 names the coconut palm tree.
耶 (yé) gives a sound close to 椰's reading yē, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 椰子里有很多椰汁。
example.pinyin: Yēzi lǐ yǒu hěn duō yēzhī.
example.english: There's a lot of coconut juice inside a coconut.
example.fact: 椰 names the coconut palm, whose fruit is unusual among plant seeds for being able to float and survive weeks at sea, letting coconut palms colonize new tropical shores across oceans.

components.note: 瓦 (pottery/tile) — 甄's original meaning involved making pottery, later extended to 'examine, discern.'
垔 (yīn) gives a sound now quite distant from 甄's reading zhēn — the phonetic link has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 公司通过面试甄选优秀的人才。
example.pinyin: Gōngsī tōngguò miànshì zhēnxuǎn yōuxiù de réncái.
example.english: The company selects outstanding talent through interviews.
example.fact: 甄 means "to examine and select carefully," as in 甄选 (zhēnxuǎn), and became broadly recognizable to modern audiences through the hit television drama 甄嬛传 (Empresses in the Palace).

meanings: toad ("chán" represents the sound of its croaking)

components.note: 虫 (creature) — 蟾 names an amphibian, the toad.
詹 (zhān) gives a sound related to 蟾's reading chán, sharing the final but with the initial consonant and tone shifted.

example.hanzi: 蟾蜍是一种两栖动物。
example.pinyin: Chánchú shì yī zhǒng liǎngqī dòngwù.
example.english: Toads are a kind of amphibian.
example.fact: In Chinese legend, a toad (蟾) is said to live on the moon alongside the more famous rabbit, giving the moon the poetic nickname 蟾宫 ("toad palace").

meanings: used in 蹊蹺|蹊跷[qi1 qiao1]

components.note: 足 (foot) — 蹊 names a footpath, a foot-related place.
奚 (xī) gives a sound close to 蹊's reading qī, sharing the final and tone but with the initial consonant shifted.

example.hanzi: 这件事有点蹊跷。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì yǒudiǎn qīqiāo.
example.english: This matter seems a bit suspicious.
example.fact: 蹊 appears mainly in 蹊跷 (qīqiāo), a colloquial word for something that seems suspicious or "off," often used when a situation doesn't add up.

etymologyHint: Still 宁 water 氵; 宁 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 氵 (water) — represents water; 泞 describes waterlogged, muddy ground.
宁 (calm, still) — combined with 'water,' suggests stagnant water pooling into mud. 宁 (níng) is also very close to 泞's reading nìng, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 下雨后路很泥泞。
example.pinyin: Xiàyǔ hòu lù hěn nínìng.
example.english: After it rains, the road is very muddy.
example.fact: 泞 appears almost only in 泥泞 (nínìng), the standard word for muddy, slushy ground after rain, a common complaint about unpaved rural roads.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 撸 describes an action done with the hand.
鲁 (lǔ) gives a sound close to 撸's reading lū, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 周末我们一起去撸串吧。
example.pinyin: Zhōumò wǒmen yīqǐ qù lūchuàn ba.
example.english: Let's go eat skewers together this weekend.
example.fact: 撸 is trendy modern slang, most famous in 撸串 (lūchuàn, literally "to pull skewers"), the casual way young Chinese people describe going out for grilled meat skewers with friends.

components.note: 虫 (creature) — 螃 names a crustacean, the crab.
旁 (páng) gives the sound — an exact match with 螃's reading.

example.hanzi: 秋天是吃螃蟹的最好季节。
example.pinyin: Qiūtiān shì chī pángxiè de zuìhǎo jìjié.
example.english: Autumn is the best season for eating crab.
example.fact: 螃 appears only in 螃蟹 (pángxiè, "crab"), and autumn is considered the prime season for eating crab in China, especially the prized 大闸蟹 ("hairy crab") from the Yangtze River delta.

meanings: used in 檸檬|柠檬[ning2 meng2]

components.note: 木 (tree) — 檬 originally named a type of tree, later reused phonetically for 'lemon.'
蒙 (méng) gives the sound — an exact match with 檬's reading.

example.hanzi: 柠檬很酸。
example.pinyin: Níngméng hěn suān.
example.english: Lemons are very sour.
example.fact: 柠檬 (níngméng, "lemon") is a phonetic loanword — unlike most Chinese fruit names, which describe the fruit's qualities (香蕉, "fragrant banana"), it was borrowed mainly for its sound rather than built from meaningful native characters.

components.note: 犭 (animal) — 猓 names an animal, a type of monkey in classical texts.
果 (guǒ) gives the sound — an exact match with 猓's reading.

example.hanzi: 古书中记载"猓"是一种长尾猿。
example.pinyin: Gǔshū zhōng jìzài "guǒ" shì yī zhǒng chángwěi yuán.
example.english: Ancient texts record that "guǒ" refers to a kind of long-tailed monkey.
example.fact: 猓 is one of the rarest characters in modern usage, surviving only in classical texts describing types of monkeys — a good example of a character that exists almost entirely as a historical relic rather than living vocabulary.

meanings: used in 薔薇|蔷薇[qiang2 wei1]

components.note: 艹 (plant) — 蔷 names a flowering plant, the rose.
啬 (sè) gives a sound now quite distant from 蔷's reading qiáng — the phonetic link has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 花园里种着蔷薇。
example.pinyin: Huāyuán lǐ zhòngzhe qiángwēi.
example.english: Roses are planted in the garden.
example.fact: 蔷 appears only in 蔷薇 (qiángwēi), the general term for wild or climbing roses, distinct from 玫瑰 (méiguī), which usually refers to cultivated garden roses given as gifts.

meanings: same as Fuxi 伏羲[Fu2 xi1], a mythical emperor

example.hanzi: 伏羲是中国神话中的人类始祖之一。
example.pinyin: Fúxī shì Zhōngguó shénhuà zhōng de rénlèi shǐzǔ zhī yī.
example.english: Fuxi is one of the mythical ancestors of humanity in Chinese mythology.
example.fact: 羲 appears almost only in the name 伏羲 (Fuxi), a legendary culture hero in Chinese mythology credited with inventing writing, fishing nets, and the Eight Trigrams used in the I Ching.

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — 瘸 describes lameness, a physical impairment.
加 (jiā) gives a sound now quite distant from 瘸's reading qué — the phonetic link has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 他腿受伤了,走路一瘸一拐的。
example.pinyin: Tā tuǐ shòushāngle, zǒulù yī qué yī guǎi de.
example.english: His leg was injured, and he walks with a limp.
example.fact: 瘸 describes lameness or a limp, most vividly in the phrase 一瘸一拐 (yī qué yī guǎi), describing someone limping unevenly with each step.

etymologyHint: To perform a rite 醮 again (like a perennial 艹)

components.note: 艹 (plant) — plants regrow each year, evoking the idea of repetition.

醮 (a ceremonial rite) — combined with the idea of regrowth, suggests repeating or dipping again, giving 蘸 its meaning "to dip." 醮 (jiào) is also historically linked to 蘸's pronunciation, though the modern reading zhàn has drifted from it.

example.hanzi: 吃饺子的时候,可以蘸一点醋。
example.pinyin: Chī jiǎozi de shíhou, kěyǐ zhàn yīdiǎn cù.
example.english: When eating dumplings, you can dip them in a bit of vinegar.
example.fact: 蘸 describes dipping food into a sauce or condiment, most commonly in 蘸酱 (zhànjiàng, "dipping sauce"), an essential step for dishes like dumplings and hot pot.

components.note: 艹 (plant) — 蔗 names a plant, sugarcane.
庶 (shù) gives a sound related to 蔗's reading zhè, sharing the tone but with the initial consonant and vowel shifted.

example.hanzi: 甘蔗汁很甜。
example.pinyin: Gānzhè zhī hěn tián.
example.english: Sugarcane juice is very sweet.
example.fact: 蔗 appears only in 甘蔗 (gānzhè, "sugarcane"), the plant that remains the world's largest source of sugar production, grown across tropical and subtropical regions including southern China.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 傀 describes a puppet, a figure resembling a person.
鬼 (guǐ) gives a sound close to 傀's reading guī, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 那个国家的政府只是外国势力的傀儡。
example.pinyin: Nàge guójiā de zhèngfǔ zhǐshì wàiguó shìlì de kuǐlěi.
example.english: That country's government is just a puppet of foreign powers.
example.fact: 傀 appears mainly in 傀儡 (kuǐlěi, "puppet"), used both literally for puppet theater and figuratively for a government secretly controlled by another power, as in 傀儡政权 ("puppet regime").

components.note: 虫 (creature) — 蚌 names a mollusk, the mussel or clam.
丰 (fēng) gives a sound now quite distant from 蚌's reading bàng — the phonetic link has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 河里可以找到河蚌。
example.pinyin: Hé lǐ kěyǐ zhǎodào hébàng.
example.english: You can find freshwater mussels in the river.
example.fact: 蚌 names freshwater mussels and clams, and the idiom 鹬蚌相争,渔翁得利 ("when the snipe and the clam fight, the fisherman profits") warns that rivals who exhaust each other let a third party win.

etymologyHint: To forge 固 metal 钅; 固 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 钅 (metal) — represents metal; 锢 originally described pouring molten metal into cracks to seal them.
固 (firm, solid) — combined with 'metal,' reinforces the sense of sealing something shut permanently. 固 (gù) is also an exact phonetic match for 锢's reading.

example.hanzi: 他被长期禁锢在家中。
example.pinyin: Tā bèi chángqī jìngù zài jiāzhōng.
example.english: He was confined at home for a long time.
example.fact: 锢 appears mainly in 禁锢 (jìngù), meaning to confine or imprison someone, whether literally, or figuratively as in 思想禁锢 ("imprisoned thinking," meaning rigid, closed-minded thought).

components.note: 辶 (walk/movement) — 遽 describes hurried, sudden movement.
豦 (jù) gives the sound — an exact match with 遽's reading.

example.hanzi: 他遽然变了脸色。
example.pinyin: Tā jùrán biànle liǎnsè.
example.english: His expression suddenly changed.
example.fact: 遽 is a literary word for "suddenly," now largely confined to formal writing and classical-style phrases like 遽然 (jùrán), while everyday speech prefers 突然 or 忽然。

components.note: 穴 (cave/hole) — 邃 describes depth, like a deep cave.
㒸 (suì) gives the sound — an exact match with 邃's reading.

example.hanzi: 他的眼神深邃而神秘。
example.pinyin: Tā de yǎnshén shēnsuì ér shénmì.
example.english: His gaze is deep and mysterious.
example.fact: 邃 appears mainly in 深邃 (shēnsuì), a literary word for something deep and profound, used equally for a deep well, deep thought, or an enigmatic gaze.

components.note: 心 (heart) — 恚 describes an emotion, rage.
圭 (guī) gives a sound now quite distant from 恚's reading huì — the phonetic link has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 他心中恚怒,却不敢言。
